YUKON QUARTZ MINING ACT-SURVEYS BY DOMINION LAND SURVEYORS
speechtext:
1.	Has the government notified the recorded owners of mineral claims that in accordance with section 78 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act they must have surveys made at their own expense by duly qualified dominion land surveyors within one year?
2.	If so, will the government reconsider the serious consequences to many small owners of mineral claims resulting from this action?

subtopic: YUKON QUARTZ MINING ACT-SURVEYS BY DOMINION LAND SURVEYORS
speechtext:
1.	Yes; this is provided by the act.
2.	The matter has already been considered. On January 7, 1948, the minister authorized the mining recorders to issue the notices contemplated by section 78 of the act. At the same time arrangements were made to have a dominion land surveyor undertake the necessary base line surveys at government expense, and the mining recorders were advised that this dominion land surveyor would survey claims for claim holders at the actual cost of the work done on each claim.
As it became evident from correspondence that the situation was not thoroughly understood, the following circular letter is being sent by the mining recorder to all those to whom notices have been given under section 78:
The correspondence which has been received as a result of the notices sent to claim holders under section 78 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act has been reported to the department and I have been instructed to furnish further information to all those to whom these notices have been sent, supplementing the information already given.
The necessity of a survey of mineral claims has been a fundamental requirement of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act from the beginning. The two-post staking system which is in effect in the Yukon Territory contemplates that there will be an early survey so that the boundary of each claim may be defined. This requirement ivas not enforced during the time when it was impossible to obtain the services of a surveyor. The net result of this leniency has been that those who wish to proceed with the development of the mineral resources of the territory are unable to ascertain the limits of the properties that can be secured either by purchase or staking.

Questions
Now that the services of dominion land surveyors are available it has been considered appropriate to require claim holders to have their claims surveyed. There is no intention of taking arbitrary action. If it is impossible to have a survey made, either because the surveyor cannot get around to it, or for good and sufficient reason the claim owner while developing his property is unable to pay the expense of the survey, then the circumstances will be considered by the minister on the representations of the claim holder.
The department is willing to do its part by improving the maps and assigning government surveyors to run the base lines. In order to assist claim holders the department is assigning a surveyor to make surveys of mineral claims. The claim holders who take advantage of this offer will be asked to make a deposit to cover the cost of the actual out of pocket expenses incidental to the survey of their claims. These expenses will not include the salary of the surveyor. It has been estimated that these charges will not exceed $200 per claim. This deposit of $200 should be made to the mining recorder, and a refund will be made should the cost be less than this amount.
It will be the responsibility of each claim holder either to have the survey of his claim made or to make the required deposit with the mining recorder. Those "who are unable to comply and who desire to establish a case for special consideration by reason of their bona fides as actual developers of the property they hold under entry should disclose the circumstances which in their opinion would justify the minister in not cancelling their claims.

subtopic: CLOSING OF CORNWALLIS VETERANS HOSPITAL, DIGBY, N.S.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CLOSING OF CORNWALLIS VETERANS HOSPITAL, DIGBY, N.S.
speechtext:
Is it the intention of the Department of Veterans Affairs to close the Cornwallis veterans hospital for tubercular patients, Digby, Nova Scotia, and transfer the patients to Camp Hill hospital, Halifax, or elsewhere? If so,
why is such action being taken, and what is to be the date of closing Cornwallis hospital?
Hon. MILTON F. GREGG (Minister of Veterans Affairs): The hon. member kindly sent me advance notice of this question. The department does intend to close the Cornwallis veterans hospital for tuberculosis patients at Digby, Nova Scotia, in the near future and transfer the patients from this hospital to Camp Hill, Halifax. The action is being taken for the following reasons:
1.	To permit a closer liaison with the medical staff at Dalhousie Medical School and so assure a continuing high standard of adequate diagnostic treatment and service to the patients.
2.	To conform to the established policy of abandoning service hospitals which were taken over temporarily to cope with the peak load as soon as suitable alternative accommodation is available in our permanent treatment centres.
3.	Bed space is available at Camp Hill hospital and structural changes are well under way to adjust this accommodation and make it suitable for the care of patients suffering from tuberculosis.
4.	The concentration of our treatment facilities in Halifax not only assures the availability of better medical care, but allows for improved treatment at a considerable reduction in over-all cost.
The exact date of closing has not been set but will be determined by the completion of the structural changes to which I have referred. The prospective date will be some time in the late summer or early fall.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO EFFECT ON CANADA'S EXCHANGE SITUATION

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, April 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley (for the Prime Minister) for the appointment of a joint committee of both houses of parliament

Human Rights
on human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the -adjournment on Friday evening I had moved an amendment with a view to having determined by the supreme court the question of the jurisdiction of the federal authority in the field of civil liberties. I hope, sir, the government will see fit to accept my suggestion, which I believe will go a long way toward determining once for all this important question, to which in 1935 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself made reference. Incidentally, just as a matter of interest, I have found in the course of reading that in 1832 the grandfather of the Prime Minister made a special trip to England for the purpose of placing before the imperial government the question of the preservation of civil liberties in Canada.
In his speech the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) referred to an article written by Doctor Humphrey, secretary of the committee on human rights. I should like to refer to another article written by the same gentleman on the subject of the international protection of human rights. It appears in the Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Sciences for January, 1948. By way of indicating the importance of an international bill of rights in which through the united nations Canada could participate and to which she could contribute, I should like to quote briefly from that article. Doctor Humphrey says this:
It is probably correct to say that there has been more public interest in the work of the commission on human rights and its various subsidiaries than in the activities of any other organ of the united nations, with the exception of the security council, although discussions in the human rights commission have seldom hit the headlines.
It goes on to indicate why the international committee has been of such importance. It states that one reason, of course, is the personality of its chairman, Mrs. Franklin Roosevelt, and that another is the realization on the part of the public of the important issues at stake. The article continues:
Not only did the peoples of the world know that world war II had been fought for human rights; they knew that the denial of human rights by certain countries had been a contributing cause of the war.
Then he uses these words:
It is significant and appropriate that this victory of the common man, this victory of private individuals, should be a victory in the age-long struggle for the definition and establishment of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I would bring that to the attention of the minister who, when he spoke the other night, made it evident that the government of this country has displayed but little interest in this important matter. Indeed an examination of the records of the united nations committee shows that all other democratic countries have made recommendations to this committee. The United States made recommendations, and the United Kingdom made recommendations in great detail, setting forth the necessity for the preservation of fundamental freedoms, as well as the sanctions that should apply.
In view of the great interest, as Doctor Humphrey says, that is being shown- throughout the world in fundamental freedoms, and the need1 for serious consideration of the subject in this country, I suggest that there be placed on Hansard the draft international declaration of human rights as well as the draft covenant. When the suggestion was made the other evening by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) the minister said that this material was too long for inclusion in Hansard. Sir, this is a declaration and covenant about which the people of this country generally know very little. I think it should appear in Hansard and thus be made available to all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I suggest that Votes and Proceedings would be a better place for it than Hansard. I would have no objection to placing it there.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That would be suitable. It should be available to every member of the house.
There are some sections which have been accepted by the committee consisting of representatives of eighteen countries. Indeed practically the only objections to many of the clauses have been from countries which are communist or under the curtain of communism.
Let me refer to three or four pertinent international human rights which this declaration would1 protect, not only internationally but also in the various nations subscribing to them. I read these in the light of some of the abrogations of civil liberties which have taken place in Canada within the last few years. These particular declarations, sir, represent the consensus of many democratic nations throughout the world; n-o communist nation has yet given any indication as to its views, although they voted against its acceptance. Here are a few articles which are regarded as of sufficient importance internationally, designed to lay the foundation for the prevention of war:
Article 3 states:
Everyone is entitled to all the rights and freedoms set forth in this declaration, without dis-
Human Rights

tinction of any kind, such as race (which includes colour), sex, language, religion, political or other opinion, property status or national or social origin.
And article 5:
No one shall be deprived of his personal liberty or kept in custody except dn eases prescribed by law and after due process.
This is particularly significant:
Everyone placed under arrest or detention shall have the right to immediate judicial determination of the legality of any detention to which he may be subject, and to trial within a reasonable time, or to release.
This section means that nations will not permit the denial of habeas corpus.
Here is another section which is of interest in view of some of the things which have happened in Canada in the last few years, particularly since the war. I quote:
Subject to any general law not contrary to the purposes and principles of the united nations charter and adopted for specific reasons of security or in general interest there shall be liberty of movement and free choice of residence within the border of each state.
There is a further one, article 16:
Individual freedom of thought and conscience to hold and change beliefs is an absolute and sacred right.
Provision is made also for the drafting of an international covenant, and it provides:
Every state, party hereto, undertakes to ensure:	(b) that such laws, respecting these
human rights and fundamental freedoms, conform with the general principles of law recognized by civilized nations;
(c)	that any person whose rights or freedoms are violated shall have an effective remedy, notwithstanding that the violation has been committed by persons acting in an official capacity.
Then:
No person shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest or detention.
How often I have said in this house that when the right to be represented by counsel is taken away, law returns to the middle ages. All these nations have agreed to this:
In the determination of any criminal charge against him or of any of his civil rights or obligations every person is entitled to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal and to the aid of a qualified representative of his own choice.
Then in regard to freedom of religion, every person shall have the right to freedom of religion, conscience and belief. The only limitations on that freedom shall be such limitations as are prescribed by law and are necessary to protect public order and welfare, morals and the rights of freedom of others.
In the event that one's fundamental freedoms have been interfered with, he should

have the right of recourse. That is why I ask that there be an amendment to the Supreme Court of Canada Act to the end that anyone in any province in Canada whose fundamental freedoms are interfered with shall have the right of determination of his rights before the Supreme Court of Canada.
My right hon. friend referred to the constitutional division between the provinces and the dominion. I should like to refer to one case which is the only one which has been before the Supreme Court of Canada in reference to the question of fundamental freedoms. There are two points of view. Some say that the right of the provinces to abrogate and interfere with the fundamental freedoms is inherent in the British North America Act, although the preamble to that act states that our constitution shall be similar to that of the United Kingdom. Those who contend that these rights rest in the provinces aver that we in this country must be a balkanized Canada whereby an individual may enjoy certain fundamental rights in one province while in another they may be denied. It is that question of legislative jurisdiction that I am asking the government of this country to submit to the supreme court. If it is the law, then it denies to the individual that Canadian citizenship which should be the result of the measure introduced by the Prime Minister in 1944. To say that in one part of Canada a Canadian may enjoy freedom of religion and of speech and of association, all those great and abiding freedoms, and that in another province a Canadian may not enjoy them, is a denial of the possibility that we shall ever build a united Canada on the basis of equality of the individual before the law in all parts of the country.
A reference was made to the supreme court with respect to an Alberta statute of 1938, as reported in the Canadian Supreme Court Reports of that year. I should like to quote from the judgments of Chief Justice Duff and Mr. Justice Cannon, which indicate that while property and civil rights are a matter for the provinces, the preservation of abiding freedoms is a matter for the parliament of Canada. The judgment of Chief Justice Duff is to be found on page 133. It will be remembered that the Alberta legislature passed' a law that denied the freedom of the press in that province.

speechtext:
That is absolutely false. I challenge the hon. member. The hon. member has no right to make remarks of that sort to this house without their being challenged.

Human Rights

speechtext:
There cannot be any controversy on that. I point out that the judgment is as follows:
The right of public discussion is, of course, subject to legal restrictions; those based upon considerations of decency and public order, and others conceived for the protection of various private and public interests with which, for example, the laws of defamation and sedition are concerned.
And further down:
We do not doubt that (in addition to the power of disallowance vested in the governor general) the parliament of Canada possesses authority to legislate for the protection of this right.
I would refer to page 134, where the chief justice points out that the freedom of the press, the right freely to express itself, is a right with which no province can interfere.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: It does not exist anyway.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not in an argumentative mood today; I am simply placing this on the record and doing it as dispassionately as I can. I hope my hon. friend will permit me to continue. On pages 145 and 146 appears the judgment of Mr. Justice Cannon, which reads:
Under the British system, which is ours, no political party can erect a prohibitory barrier to prevent the electors from getting information concerning the policy of the government. Freedom of discussion is essential to enlighten public opinion in a democratic state; it cannot be curtailed without affecting the right of the people to be informed through sources independent of the government concerning matters of public interest.
Then there are these significant, words, which have never been departed from or derogated from since 1938, by the Supreme Court:
No province lias the power to reduce in that province the political rights of its citizens as compared with those enjoyed by the citizens of other provinces of Canada.
What that means is that no province may within the ambit of property and civil rights interfere with freedom of religion or freedom of speech or freedom of the press by provincial legislation which would deny the maintenance of those freedoms. I suggest that in view of this authority of the supreme court, something should be done by this parliament to grant to the individual the right of appeal to the supreme court when his fundamental freedoms have been interfered with in any way. That case came before the supreme court, not as a result of an appeal by an individual, but on a submission by the governor in council.
The position regarding civil liberty is this. If any province can by the exercise, or by
the subterfuge of the exercise, of its licensing authority under municipal law, interfere with fundamental freedoms, and there is no recourse to the courts, the individual so interfered with, however great his freedoms may appear to be, in fact does not possess those freedoms. If being a Canadian implies the possession of fundamental and traditional freedoms, no citizen of this country should be denied the opportunity of asserting his freedoms in the courts.
With those who say that the dominion parliament has no power to pass a bill of rights I do not agree; but let us accept that for a moment. The first thing, then, that the parliament should do is to equalize the rights of Canadians everywhere in Canada, so that they can go to the foot of the throne, to the Supreme Court of Canada, and, if they will, to the privy council, when their rights have been abrogated.
If a municipal authority has the right by licensing, by imposing a licence fee, to deny the privilege of practising one's religion it then can do indirectly what it cannot do directly. I suggest to the Prime Minister as the culminating act of his career that he give to Canadians everywhere the assurance of full rights of equality in Canadian citizenship which was placed on the statute book by his government, by amending the Supreme Court Act to give the individual the right to the preservation and maintenance of his freedoms against provincial intrusion wherever it occurs.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: What intrusion?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is any imaginable number.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: If the hon. member would specifically mention one, it would be more illuminating.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will point out what happened in the United States, where the preservation of the right of freedoms was maintained by the supreme court of that country, in Murdock vs. Pennsylvania, 319 United States Reports, 103-

speechtext: But we have not been annexed yet.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What my hon. friend says is true, although there are many who say we are a satellite. But I am not dealing with that phase this afternoon. I am dealing with interference with the individual's rights and with the necessity of an amendment to the Supreme Court Act to prevent in any provincial authority or any emanation of a provincial authority the exercise of the right to
Human Rights

do by indirect means what cannot be done directly. In that case Mr. Justice Murphy of the United States supreme court used these words:
It is wise to remember that the taxing and licensing power is a dangerous and potent weapon which, in the hands of unscrupulous or bigoted men, could be used to suppress freedoms and destroy religion unless it is kept within appropriate bounds.
If being a Canadian anywhere in Canada implies equality and the possession of those traditional freedoms, then let us grant the individual the right to preserve his freedoms by having an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I pass on to the next phase, and it has to do with the international aspect of the matter. I cannot understand, sir, why it is that sor little interest has been shown by the government of this country in submitting suggestions for an international bill of rights. Over a period of two years no such recommendations have emanated from Canada. The government knew in January last what were the terms of an international bill of rights. The united nations committee forwarded to the government the draft terms in detail, and it has remained under cover all through February, March and April. It could have been tabled in the house in order to permit of consideration and discussion, but like so many other matters connected with our foreign affairs it has had to remain the secret of the government until now. That committee met. We had no representative there from Canada. The secretary was a Canadian. The committee drafted this bill of rights in two documents, a declaration and a convention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext: How can my hon. friend say it was a secret in the bosom of the government when it was published to the whole world?

speechtext: I was sent to the governments of the various countries, and sent to Canada, but if it was not a secret it has been kept under wraps and not tabled in parliament since January last.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was available long before then.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Available to whom and by whom? Not to parliament or in parliament. It is against this secrecy in connection with our foreign affairs in general that I protest.

There is a convention and a declaration; a declaration that will merely be a statement of the pious idealism of the various countries, and a convention declaring a number of rights which the several states making up the united nations will be required to enforce. When it is ratified by a two-thirds majority it will be legally binding on each state when ratified by that state. My right hon. friend indicated that there is no rush. He admitted that this matter was supposed to be considered by the various nations within the united nations by April 3, 1948, and parliament did not get it until the 8th or 9th of April. It was to be considered by the various countries and suggestions were to be made by them. Now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) suggests that we do not rush the matter, which was supposed to be dealt with next fall, but that we delay it again. Mrs. Roosevelt has written an article on the subject in the April 1948 issue of Foreign Affairs, wherein she emphasizes the necessity of action now, action before the united nations ceases to function, as it is ceasing to function in parts of the world. She indicates that the one hope for mankind is that they get together and arrive at a standard in connection with the maintenance of human rights, without which there cannot be peace.
The declaration will be merely a declaration of hope. The convention will be a declaration of civil liberties binding on the nations when accepted by them.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: It binds no one. It binds only the hon. member for Lake Centre. That declaration binds no one else.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Apparently my hon. friend, usually so well informed, has not read this. He has not had an opportunity because it is just now to be tabled. Canada's parliament and Canada generally should know what is the attitude of the Canadian government with respect to an international bill of rights. We have never yet been able to find it out. The United States took so great an interest in this matter that its state department sent out letters to 350 private organizations in the United States asking for their opinions and suggestions. The state department has publicly stated its appreciation of the suggestions given as the result of the request of the government. Canada has a position on the security council of the united nations; Canada is on the atomic control board; Canada has seats here and there; but in a matter that every one of the united nations representatives in San Francisco indicated was upon the conscience of mankind and should be epito-

Human Rights
mized in the form of a declaration, Canada does nothing. All it did was to wait while the committee had sat for a period, off and on, and at the end of three months concluded its recommendations, terminated its sittings, and agreed to meet again on May 8 or 9 of this year after further recommendations on the draft had been secured by the several nations. It does indicate, sir, if not a fear on the part of the government to face this question, at least an apathy, which, according to Doctor Humphrey, whom the minister quoted as an authority on the subject, is not to be found among the other nations who are interested in the preservation of the united nations.
I ask the minister this: has parliament not the right to know whether Canada is to be bound by the convention? Has it taken up with the provinces the question as to the degree to which correlative and complementary legislation will be passed? If not, Canada will be in the position of being not in the vanguard but in the rearguard of the march on the part of the nations of the world to these better things conducive of international peace.
I come next to the question of freedom of the press. This is a subject which has been before the people of Canada in very recent days. The preservation above all things of that freedom is so fundamental that without its preservation, parliament cannot function or democracy operate in the interest of the people. Now that a decision has been arrived at, the minister should give early attention to what I suggested some weeks ago, namely, amending section 888 of the criminal code so that never again will publishers, writers or authors be subject to being taken from one end of Canada to the other at the whim or desire of any group.
All along the road mankind has had to fight for freedom of the press as for other freedoms. Freedom of the press was first established in 1771 in the John Wilkes case. In the diastole and systole of history, the freedom of the press, though diminished from time to time, has been maintained in the main. It is for that reason that one of the chief committees set up by the united nations committee on human rights was the committee on freedom of the press. That committee has just reported. Canada had representatives on the committee, which met in Geneva. Free discussion is fundamental for the preservation of the principles for which we stand. Experience shows that man will speak the things he will within the law, regardless of the punishment that may be levied against him for so doing. Preservation of our freedoms lies in the right of every man under law to express
his point of view, limited only by sedition, blasphemy and libel. When I hear people talking about repression and denying a man the right to think the things he will under law, I am amazed. They believe that all you have to do to prevent the spread of false philosophies is to bring in laws that will deny the right to free speech. In doing so they deny the preservation of the thing that by repression they believe they are preserving. The only effective answer to the propagation of false philosophies is to assure to every citizen information on what are the abiding principles of freedom. They will recognize their superiority over those false doctrines, those godless doctrines, those doctrines that would destroy the relationship between a man and his God and the sacredness of his personality.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: What false doctrines?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I speak now of the doctrine of communism.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will you please enumerate?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I speak of the doctrine of communism; I hope I have my hon. friend's agreement. The freedom to destroy false doctrines is to have the right to speak against them. When I hear people say how they would control false doctrines I say that we need in this country those who will exercise the right to freedom of speech and show our people what freedom means, what are its abiding principles and its superiority over doctrines which result in the blackout of freedom and the maintenance of tyranny everywhere in the world.
Yesterday I came on a quotation from a speech which was delivered in the British House of Commons a hundred and fifty years ago. It is now repeated in the declaration on freedom of the press made a few days ago by the thirty nations meeting in Geneva. One hundred and fifty years ago Sheridan used these words:
Give me but the liberty of the press and I will concede to the government a corrupt and servile House of Commons. I "will give ministers the full swing of the patronage of office. I will give them a whole host of ministerial influence. I will give all the power that can be conferred to purchase submission and overawe resistance. And yet armed with the liberty of the press I will go forth to meet them undismayed. I will attack the mighty fabric government has reared with that mightier engine. I will shake down from its heights corruption and bury it beneath the ruins of the abuses it was meant to shelter.
What have we done in this nation with regard to that committee and the maintenance of the freedom of the press? Thirty-five nations were represented on the committee. Five of them voted against the preservation of
Human Rights

the freedom of the press. Those five consisted of the U.S.S.R. and its satellite nations, the Ukraine, Czechoslovakia, Poland and Yugoslavia. The thirty nations agreed that we must preserve these freedoms, and the greatest of these, to assure the penetration of the iron curtain, is the freedom to distribute news everywhere in the world without regard to country or opposition in any country. They said:
Freedom of information carries the right to gather, transmit and disseminate news anywhere. Freedom of information depends for its validity on the availability and diversity of sources of news and opinion.
Then the committee set out the responsibilities and the duties of the press. It says this:
The press has a moral obligation to seek the truth and report the facts, thereby contributing to a solution of the world's problems.
If the minister is to be the chairman of this
committee I should like him to bring before it representatives who have attended on behalf of Canada at this press gathering in Geneva, to the end that we in this country will have presented to our people something of the appeal that was made to these men as to the necessity of preserving as a federal responsibility freedom of the press everywhere in this country.
There are some who contend that when yqu speak of freedom in the world today you speak of an anachronism. By freedom do you mean the absence of law? Do you imply that freedom is the absence of direction? Those things are not freedom. Some there are in our own country who fear freedom. Others there are who believe they should have the freedom to do the thing they desire to do, but that someone else should be denied that same right under the law. To me freedom means the recognition of my right as a person within the state to equality under the law; and my right to the maintenance of fundamental freedoms which are our heritage. That heritage can be preserved only when there are rules which require the other person, in my interests and in his, to keep within the rules. It implies that each must be restricted by the existence of equal rights for others.
Equality for all has not been characteristic of some of the actions of this government during the years since the war. I am trying to keep away from any suggestion of political considerations in this discussion. But I say- and I do so without fear of there being anyone who will seriously deny it-that within the last two or three years in our country there has been an unnecessary continuance of invasions of the fundamental freedoms belonging to our

people. In 1932 the Prime Minister himself summarized the danger. Speaking in this house, he warned the country of the dangers of arbitrary authority. These words I bring to his attention and to that of his government today:
Arbitrary authority helps breed arbitrary authority. The enjoyment of a certain amount of absolute power creates the appetite for more power in the way of absolute power and finally absolutism knows no bounds.
This government was in power during the second world war. All of us were willing to surrender rights which were fundamental, in the greater interest of the survival and preservation of the state. But, with the conclusion of the war, in too many cases the government has continued to abrogate our rights, no doubt soothed by the fact that in the days of war we submitted willingly and voluntarily. When I observe the actions of some of the ministers in the cabinet I ask myself if these men are engaged in a competition among themselves for absolute power. Some show a greed for power. Some show that they are afflicted with the violence of unrestrained authority outside the law. I refer only to what happened recently when the imposition of taxes in our country was announced by radio speech. No one denied that it was an abrogation of the principles of Magna Carta. The minister could not do it. Following Magna Carta, because of the inclination on the part of some people to depart from its principles, a curse was placed on all who departed from them. According to the author I read, no king's minister, no cabinet minister, no adviser or person who departed from those principles would ever be able to remove himself from the curse that was pronounced, namely, that he would be driven out of power or restrained by the people. I shall read what that curse was. It condemned every official of the state sworn to uphold it, and-
"All those that by word, deed or counsel-in any point, break or undo" its provisions or who "in any manner" procure, counsel or any way assent to resist or break them or "to go about it, by word or deed, openly or secretly, by any manner of pretence or colour."
Some people say: You have Magna Carta; what more do you want? The great principles of Magna Carta are abiding, permanent, eternal. What right has any individual in this country, if the federal government decides to do away with his right to appeal to the courts to have its principles preserved for him? In connection with the imposition of taxation outside of parliament, John Hampden in 1628 was approached by the representatives of the king who said, "Well, forget about it;

Human Rights
after all, it is just one departure. Pay it up." His answer was, "That I dare not do, for I fear to draw upon myself the curse in Magna Carta." What Hampden remembered in 1628 was apparently forgotten by the government of Canada in 1947. Why do we need a bill of rights in this country? I am not going to quote to you what the papers that do not support the government have to say; I refer you, Mr. Speaker, to what the Winnipeg Free Press said as late as February 26, 1948:
The remedy,-
It refers to invasions by this government of the rights of individuals that have continued since the war.
-in good part at least, lies with the dominion parliament and some action is being taken.
Then it points out the necessity for action.
No civil liberties legislation exists in Canada to protect the fundamental freedoms of Canadians. In the past it has been assumed that the liberal tradition and the vigilance of an alert electorate would suffice to protect them, but recent experience shows that this is only too obviously not so. Within a decade or a little more, serious inroads have been made upon the rights of Canadians.
That is in 1948, written in a paper which generally gives support to the government. It points out the necessity for a bill of rights which will assure not only the maintenance of fundamental freedoms but the right of the individual, under law, to recourse to the courts in order to have those rights preserved.
In England within the last few months an anomaly has been removed; the crown may now be sued in the courts of the land just as an individual may be sued in those courts. In this country the federal government is in business on a scale not exceeded by Great Britain. I am not going to enumerate the businesses it is in. No citizen has any right to recourse to the courts against the crown, except by leave of the crown. I suggest that the time has come to remove this anomaly from the law in our country. I go further and point out the unfairness which was exhibited by this government two years ago when a man in western Canada, Mr. Oatway, instituted an action against the wheat board for certain rights he contended were his. He got into the courts and went as far as the court of appeal of Manitoba; he had the right to take proceedings, but what did this government do? When he decided to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada this government, which asserts that it believes in fundamental freedoms, had an order in council passed denying him the right to appeal to that court, and also denying him the right ever to have commenced the action he legally started. I say, sir, that- is a serious matter.
It indicates that some members of this government believe they and those under them are above the law. This is the sort of thing that parliament can and should correct. You may ask whether this is the situation only in Canada. It is not.

speechtext: Would not the hon. member consider that the tying up of the distribution of scores of millions of dollars to the farmers, which would have resulted if that matter had gone on, was something that should be considered?

speechtext:
Oh, sir, that is exactly the point I want to make. Whenever this government infringes upon fundamental freedoms it says, in effect, that you have the right but in the interests of the state we are denying you the right we state you have. That principle of ex post facto legislation is denied in the united nations draft. It is a most dangerous form of legislation, to come along after the event and by law deny the individual his right in court.
I want to read now what the Marquess of Reading said when he introduced the bill of rights in the British House of Lords in 1947. He pointed out these continuing invasions which are taking place, with government divesting itself of control by parliament, and infringing upon the rights of the individual beyond what is necessary for the preservation of the state. At page 763 of the House of Lords Hansard the Marquess of Reading dealt with this matter in these words.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: What date, please?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It was in February of 1947. I have not the date here, but it appears at page 763 of the House of Lords debates:
Personal freedom had for so long been the current coin of life in this country that we had been apt perhaps to forget that currency may be slowly and stealthily withdrawn from circulation, that coinage may be debased without any very evident outward signs, and it may even be deliberately counterfeited without immediate detection.
It is not part of my case today to allege any malign conspiracy on the part of anyone deliberately to attempt to overthrow the liberties of the subject. The process has been gradual, stealthy, haphazard, almost inadvertent, but unfortunately both insidious and menacing in its cumulative effect. The pace and the magnitude of events have in recent years been filched and liberties purloined almost without the notice of parliament or the knowledge of the public.
The earlier parts of the bill he introduced- which incidentally passed the House of Lords-
-are, therefore, directed to the remedying of two evil tendencies; the growing usurpation by
Human Rights

the executive powers of parliament, and the increasing exclusion of the courts of law from what is perhaps their supreme function-protecting the individual citizens against the excessive and illegitimate encroachments and abuses of authority. These tendencies are, unhappily, no new feature of our life. They have now been nurtured upon the special conditions of emergency obtaining throughout two long, arduous and fluctuating wars.
What do I suggest should be done? My suggestion, sir, is that in view of the importance of civil liberties and their preservation, there be set up a standing committee of the House of Commons on civil rights. The recommendation has been made in the British parliament-and while it has not been accepted yet I understand it was very favourably received-that a committee be set up which meet continually and have for its responsibility the examination of all orders in council, statutes and the like that deny the individual the right of recourse to the courts. Such a clearing house committee would be of great benefit. It would reveal to the people as a whole the trend that is taking place, and would create a well informed social concern. That committee would be a vigilant upholder, through publicity, of the rights of the individual. Recently when the Prime Minister moved the appointment of the prices committee he said one of its great functions would be publicity. Surely if in economic matters publicity will cure evil, in the matter of one's freedoms it would also be an advantage if a committee such as this were set up; for, sir, as Mr. Justice Douglas of the United States supreme court said in a recent judgment:
The extent of a community's respect of the human rights of all its citizens is in fact the measure of its progress in civilization.
This committee would correlate information regarding interferences with civil liberties as they take place. It would give publicity thereto. It would make Canadians everywhere cognizant and constantly aware of invasions of our basic liberties and of the inadequacy, in many cases, of our present laws in guarding those liberties. It would make Canadians freedom-conscious, for this committee would provide parliament with a watching brief over freedom regardless of what may be the distribution of powers under the British North America Act.

The denial of the right of counsel should be removed in every case and in every statute. It has not been denied in Britain since 1652. If a citizen is denied the right of access to the courts against the decision of a cabinet minister, the minister

is placed in the position that he is able to usurp the rights of the individual and protect wrongdoers who are acting for the crown.
These are only a few matters which in my view deserve the attention of my right hon. friend as Minister of Justice. He, after all, is the conscience of justice of the Canadian people. He is the person in whose custody and subject to whose control reposes and rests the preservation of fundamental freedom. Civil rights and their preservation are the cornerstones of* liberty. All history and our own experiences recently in Canada have shown that these rights are not safe in the hands of the executive when the individual has no right to challenge their legality in the courts.
Let us resolve once for all the doubts that
are expressed as to who has the custody of the preservation of these rights. If they are in the dominion, let us in this parliament do our part toward their preservation. If they are in the provinces, then so far as an international and national bill of rights is concerned, if Canada is to take her place internationally and nationally the provinces will have to assume their responsibility in passing complementary legislation.
This is not a matter for partisanship. Freedom is an abiding thing. It is the heritage which we inherited. Freedom is your right and my right to equality under law. It is your right and my right to respect each other's rights under law.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened to an argument in favour of the adoption by this parliament of a comprehensive bill of rights. The amendu ment which has been moved requests that the legal and constitutional position of the dominion and the provinces shall be clarified. With the subject matter of the amendment I am in agreement. I want to say to my hon. friend that while I agree with much of what he has said, indeed with almost all of it, yet I rather think that he tends to overlook something. Recourse to the courts is not always as he suggests it is under various statutes of Canada. As a matter of fact some people are denied access to the courts because they cannot afford to pay the amounts that must necessarily be paid or that are involved in carrying actions right through to their ultimate conclusion. Until that disability has been removed, there is no equality in access to the courts; there is no equality before the law.
I think that is one of the reasons wffiy the workmen's compensation acts are as they are today. The workmen knew that in fighting powerful and wealthy corporal ions for com-

Human Rights
pensation they would be at a distinct disadvantage under certain circumstances. Consequently these acts are drafted as they are.
This is an important committee. I had the privilege, along with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), of attending the San Francisco conference and, jointly with him, being a member of the committee which dealt with certain clauses of the charter of the united nations which have a material bearing on this whole issue.
The committee is being established for the purpose of recommending what steps should be taken in Canada for preserving or extending respect for the observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms. I want to say that I make no apology for supporting the setting up of a committee of that description. I make no apology for supporting a move to give greater human rights and better fundamental freedoms.
The party with which I am associated in this house shares the long tradition of the workers' movements throughout the world for improved social and economic conditions, for greater freedom and more fundamental rights for humanity. My mind goes back this afternoon, particularly as I heard the hon. gentleman speaking, to the Chartist movement and to 1848, which is sometimes called in out history the year of European revolutions. I remember how that was followed by the long struggle for the right to vote, the long struggle for the universal franchise, the long struggle for the secret ballot and the periodic election of representatives to parliaments. Out of that struggle arose some of the great movements that have made for greater freedom; the trade unions, for example, the cooperative societies and other peoples' movements which we take for granted in the world in which wre are living today. The very basis of the party which I represent here this afternoon, the very basis of democratic socialism is to be found in the legislation which has been adopted through the pressure of ordinary people in all the countries of the world. Those aims were written into the charter of the united nations, a copy of which I hold in my hand. Article 55 reads;
With a view to the creation of conditions of stability and well-being which are necessary for peaceful and friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples, the united nations shall promote:
a.	higher standards of living, full employment, and conditions of economic and social progress and development:
b.	solutions of international economic, social, health, and related problems; and international cultural and educational co-operation; and
5849-182i
c.	universal respect for, and observance of, human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion.
When we signed the charter of the united nations we approved article 56, which reads:
All members pledge themselves to take joint and separate action in co-operation with the organization for the achievement of the purposes set forth in article 55.
Partly because of article 56 we are taking the action we are taking here today, the setting up of a committee to see how in Canada we can bring about conditions that are more in conformity with the aims and obligations of the united nations. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) in San Francisco in 1945 put their signatures to the charter of the united nations they obligated us not only to set up a committee but to take appropriate action when the committee reports to the house. True, of course, in these days there have been what I might call perversions of the meaning of both the words "democracy" and "socialism". Human rights and fundamental freedoms are being denied in the name of both to millions of people in some parts of the world. But this is not the first time in history that great words, great expressions, great phrases and great ideas have been perverted. Take the history of the Christian religion. Looking back over its long history, we recall how in the name of Christianity from time to time liberties were restricted, freedom of speech and of thought prohibited, and persecutions took place, with war, burnings at the stake and all the rest of it, not by one nation against another but by varying religions against other religions. But these events did not destroy the fundamental value of the Christian religion, nor can any perversion of democracy or of socialism today interfere with the basic rightness of those ideals and -the basic struggle which they involve for human freedom and human good.
So I say that the party with which I am associated is proud to support every move for greater social and economic freedom. But I also say that until we have achieved economic freedom we have not completely achieved a democratic society. As a matter of fact today in this house we are apt to discuss only one side of this problem of freedom. What are the fundamental rights every human being should enjoy?
First I say that every human being, regardless of race, colour, creed, religion, sex, or ethnic origin should have the right to pursue his or her work, to earn a decent living, and
Human Rights

to enjoy the fruits of labour; also to have the opportunity for spiritual and cultural development in conditions of dignity and of freedom. Until we have guaranteed economic freedom, with all that it implies, we have not secured the conditions which provide either for good employment or for proper cultural and spiritual development. I say that this involves more than the elimination of the terrible menace of unemployment, that sense of insecurity which haunts many a worker from the cradle to the grave. It means the right to a voice in the management of industry, as well as the right to organize and bargain collectively, for how free is the individual until he has some say as to the conditions under which he labours in industry and gets his living? I want to express that thought in the words of a great Christian socialist, the late Archbishop of Canterbury, Doctor William Temple, who wrote in his little book, Christianity and Social Order, a paragraph which I remember reading at the time and which strikes a note in my memory today. He said:
The great lack is the absence of any voice in the control or direction of the concern to which most of the -waking hours of the day are given. Till this can be remedied there will be one most important respect in which the -working class is shut out from a vitally important expression of personality. Men have fought and died for a voice in making the laws which they are to obey; that is the essence of political liberty. But the government of the firm for which he works affects a man's life more closely than the government of his state; yet in it he has no part except so far as he may threaten to hold up the process by withdrawing his labour and that of his fellow-workers in a strike. In many businesses nowadays the workers are often consulted, especially about regulations affecting hours and conditions of work. So far, so good; but this is done as a favour and not as a matter of secured right. The cause of freedom will not be established till political freedom is fulfilled in economic freedom.
Moreover, until this is done, the breach in the fellowship-of which the class-war is the ultimate expression-must remain. It is important to remember that the class-war was not first proclaimed as a crusade by Marx and Engels, it was first announced as a fact by Adam Smith. Nothing can securely end it except the acquisition by labour of -a share in the control of industry.
That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the fundamental rights, one of the fundamental freedoms, that is often overlooked in a debate of this kind. While I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) that we should write into our constitution a bill of rights safeguarding our political liberties we shall never have full freedom and full fundamental rights until the dignity of every man is recognized and until every man's right to a say in the conditions under which he

works and lives has been established. These are some of the basic rights which in my opinion have yet to be achieved, basic rights which to a very large extent through being denied are responsible for the great wave of unrest that is passing across the world. I believe with the late Archbishop Temple that until we have given recognition to the dignity of the worker in relation to his own industry we shall never meet the threat of that class war which threatens us today. Indeed once you give that right, you banish the very reason for such a class war, because then the worker will be in a position to control his own destiny in common with others m the community.
Freedom of association and freedom of expression, as my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre so well said this afternoon, we have been in danger of losing through what I think were ill-advised actions of the government during the lifetime of this parliament. The government knows what I am now thinking of. It is not only that kind of action which jeopardizes our fundamental freedoms, but the kind of action that is sometimes encouraged by people who have not thought the matter through when they approve mob violence in any form. I regret sincerely that within the last few weeks we have seen violence against political leaders and a political party whose fundamental principles I cordially detest. Nonetheless, if we condone violence against parties we dislike the time may come when the very procedure that we have condoned may be used against all the rest of us. We cannot afford ever to pass over lightly any violation of those freedoms which we enjoy.
If I may use this as an illustration, Great Britain at the present time is probably the nation, certainly in the European continental orbit, with the least danger from either fascism or communism. I was over there twice during the war. I went to the Hyde Park comer where I saw the utmost freedom of speech. The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), the hon member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and I went there one evening. There was a crowd of soldiers and sailors of various nationalities, British, American, Polish, and so on around there. We heard a speaker denouncing the war and calling upon the people to stop what he called the bloody slaughter. He was telling them how they would be fooled once more when the war was over. All the time a policeman was walking around seeing that there was no interference and no attempt at interference. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the more freedom of speech we have, the less danger there will be of subversive elements destroying our democratic institutions. Therefore I say that these recent disturbances have been very dis-

Human Rights
quieting to those of us who believe in freedom. They are symptomatic of dangerous tendencies which, being allowed to grow, may have dire results. After all, if violence is used against those who believe in violence- because both the fascist and communist parties fundamentally believe that the only way to secure control of the state eventually is by the forcible overthrow of the state-we invite and justify their violence later on. We must see that we do not jeopardize our fundamental freedom in that regard.
Then sometimes we have ill-considered legislation. My hon. friend mentioned some this afternoon. Very recently we have had an ill-considered piece of legislation which has done more to play into the hands of subversive elements than anything that has happened in Canada for a long time. I refer to the recent legislation passed in Prince Edward Island dealing with labour unions, outlawing national unions and international unions, excepting only those that are connected with the railways. When you attempt to interfere with the right of labour to organize freely in associations of its own choice as Canadian citizens all across Canada in co-operation with their fellow Canadians you are inviting serious trouble, and you are placing in the hands of those who wish to point out that governments will destroy labour unions whenever the opportunity and necessity arises, an argument which, as long as legislation of that description remains on the statute books, you cannot meet. Therefore I say that we must beware lest legislation of that description is allowed to stand. Consequently I am glad that the committee on industrial relations has also been set up and that a national labour code will be considered.
I should like to see a code which gives every Canadian wherever he may live the right to organize and bargain collectively. It requires, as do some other matters with which my hon. friend dealt this afternoon, some complementary legislation, some understanding between the provinces and the dominion about their respective powers; but every effort should be made to see to it that every Canadian worker has full rights as a Canadian citizen.
We have seen the rights of minorities interfered with. Goodness knows I have no connection with or sympathy for the teachings of, for example, Jehovah's Witnesses. Particularly I have no sympathy for some of the propaganda and their statements; but I view with considerable misgivings attempts to crush out a religious minority and to prevent their discussing religious issues from their point of view. Surely the rest of us who do not believe in the kind of teachings which they present to the Canadian people have enough faith in
our own religious bodies to be able to meet the criticisms that they level against the churches -and I use the plural because all our churches are criticized by Jehovah's Witnesses-to which we collectively or severally belong. Therefore I say that we have to beware lest we permit the persecution of minorities; because if we do we are false to the fundamentals of human freedom, of fundamental human rights, and we are false to the very charter which our representatives signed at San Francisco and which this parliament subsequently approved.
We have as well the blot on our statute books which we of this party tried to remove again this year, namely, the continuance of disabilities against a group of Canadians who are of a different race and different colour from our own, I refer to Canadians of Japanese origin. I might also say that we have not yet removed all the disabilities against another group, the Chinese residents of this country, who do not enjoy the same privileges as residents of other nationalities within this country. Until we have removed these blots on our escutcheon, we shall find it difficult to face the committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms of the united nations. In fact, when I was there in the autumn of 1946 and some of these matters were under discussion, to a minor extent, I know that all the members, irrespective of party, of the Canadian delegation felt very conscious of the manner in which we ourselves were situated when some of these topics came before the assembly or were mentioned by representatives of other nations.
I say that we have to beware lest we ourselves are guilty of that which we condemn. We should remove from our statute books and from our country all the disabilities which afflict individuals merely because they are of a different race, different colour or different religion. I know, too, that there are parts of Canada -where people of different racial origin find it difficult to get hotel and other accommodation. That is -a disgrace in Canada in 1948. The hon. member for Lake Centre mentioned freedom of the press. That is a precious heritage. No one who has read that wonderful tract by John Milton, the "Areo-pagitica", a plea for the liberty of the press, can fail to understand that his plea referred to one of the very bases of our fundamental freedoms. John Wilkes came along later, and after arrest and trial he established the right to criticize the crown's ministers, to report the debates of parliament and to say what he would about public questions. Freedom of the press? I say freedom from censorship of
Human Rights

books, of the press and of art, except only to the extent made necessary by the requirements of morality and of decency. There should be no other form of censorship except that we should see to it that decency and morality are protected. I remember an amusing incident which occurred a few years ago in the city in which I lived. A friend of mine sent to a secondhand book store in Britain to get some books. When they arrived, he received all the books except one. The book he did not receive was sent to Ottawa to see if it was a fit one for him to read. The book was "Socialism, Critical and Constructive", by James Ramsay MacDonald who at that time was Prime Minister of Britain.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Peel is a distinguished citizen of a province in which his own party laid fairly wide foundations of public ownership which will be extremely useful later on when we come to extend public ownership in the form we advocate. I refer, of course, to the hydro electric system of Ontario.

I wish to raise a question of order, Mr. Speaker; I am not taking part in the debate. On Friday evening the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved an amendment to the resolution in the words which are to be found at page 2847 of Hansard for April 9. My submission is that the amendment is not in order, for two or three reasons.
In the first place it is in essence a separate motion rather than an amendment. The motion itself is to set up a committee, and it prescribes the terms of reference to that committee. If this amendment had sought to add to the duties or functions or purposes of the committee it would have been in order. Instead of that, it seeks to cast a duty upon the executive of the government of Canada, and therefore in essence is a separate motion and not an amendment.
Secondly, and I submit this ground with great confidence, the amendment would cast upon the Supreme Court of Canada the duty of doing what the committee is to be appointed to do. One of the duties of the committee is to consider what is the legal
and constitutional situation in Canada with respect to such rights. The object of the amendment is to take that function away from the committee and place it instead with the Supreme Court of Canada. If that reference were made to the supreme court the matter would then become sub judice and the committee would be unable, during the time the matter was being considered by the supreme court, to consider what is the legal and constitutional situation in Canada with respect to such rights. The two objects cannot co-exist in the same resolution. Then the resolution would say the committee is to determine what is the legal and constitutional situation in Canada with respect to such rights, and the amendment would say that for a period at least, while it is assumed the committee will be sitting, the Supreme Court of Canada is to consider that very question.
I think there are other grounds as well but I shall not mention them. I just want to say that the two grounds I have raised are without prejudice to such other grounds as may exist; but I submit these two grounds, and certainly the second one, with confidence.

Before the point of order was raised this afternoon, I had given consideration to the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and, in that connection, had prepared the following ruling:
The main motion proposes that a select committee be set up to consider, inter alia, what is the legal and constitutional situation in Canada with respect to human rights and fundamental freedoms. The hon. member for Lake Centre has moved in amendment that in order to assist the committee in its deliberations the government immediately submit to the Supreme Court of Canada such questions as are necessary to determine to what extent the preservation of the fundamental freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly and the maintenance of constitutional safeguards of the individual are matters of federal jurisdiction.
This amendment actually proposes that the supreme court be asked to consider the same matter that the main motion proposes to refer to a select committee. It seems to me that both those propositions cannot be approved at the same time by the house. If the constitutional situation of human rights is submitted to the supreme court it thereby becomes sub judice and cannot be considered by the committee until the court has given its decision. The question cannot be before two public bodies at the same time. For this reason I feel bound to rule the amendment out of order.

I am not so much impressed by arguments which have been used by those who advocate the need for a bill of rights for Canada. We talk about freedom of speech; we talk about freedom of religion and freedom of association; but I am always inclined to ask myself which of these freedoms we have lost, or which of them we are in danger of losing.
Have we not always had these freedoms; do they not still exist? The only freedom which people in this country have not realized is economic freedom. And when one proposes a way in which that freedom could be established, his proposal is taboo. In what way are our human rights and fundamental freedoms endangered today? To hear some speak, one would be almost led to the conclusion that the present administration must be on the verge of taking some of those freedoms from us. Of course in time of war we have witnessed the government exercising certain controls which were necessary in wartime. We have delegated, by legislation, the power to the present government to institute those controls. We have been waiting patiently for the government to release them since the war.
That release may not be taking place as quickly as some of us might wish. Personally, however, I cannot quite believe that the present administration desires to take away from Canadians their human rights and fundamental freedoms. I have been sitting in this corner of the house for about thirteen years looking at pretty much the same faces on the treasury benches. I have opposed much that they have proposed; but I cannot quite bring myself to the belief that they are so lax in their loyal Canadianism that they would interfere today with the human rights and fundamental freedoms of Canadians.
I have associated with my Conservative friends. They may some time or another take over the reins of office. They may not have a solution for the economic freedom of the nation, but I am quite sure that if they were in office they would not assume their responsibilities with any idea of curtailing our human rights and fundamental freedoms.

In the first place, Mr. Speaker, we must state the question and try to understand what is meant by liberty and freedom. My understanding of liberty is that it is the faculty of man to act within the limits of the law. It is a general definition, but there is not absolute liberty in this world. Ever
since the Ten Commandments were given to man, there have been restrictions on his liberty. The object of the civil law-and in using that expression I take it in a broad sense; I mean the purpose of all laws made by man-is just to help man to act in conformity with the Ten Commandments. This is the principle of all legislation. Naturally there is too much of it and there are hindrances as a result of the excess of legislation. But I still persist in saying that freedom is the faculty given to man to act within the law.
There are, of course, some good laws and some bad ones. That is inevitable. That goes with the freedom of man. But law is conducive to order. The purpose of law is to maintain order, because order is the most desirable condition of society; and order in society is to be appreciated by men as the normal condition of affairs. When some men act as termites to destroy the pillars of state and to destroy order, that order must be maintained in spite of the efforts of the few to destroy it. This is why sanctions are necessary in order to maintain order in any well organized state. It is not a pleasure to pay taxes for the support of policemen, but it is done in all civilized countries in order that the laws shall be respected. There are constables at the various doors of this building. They do not arrest anybody. They are here just in case something wrong happens and just to maintain order and to restore order if ever it is disturbed.
There are some people who have more sympathy with those who destroy the order of society than with those who abide by the law. It is their right to think in that way, but it is my right to tell them that they are wrong. I remember the time during the war when people were so enthusiastic-at least, some of them were-in defending the liberties of the people that they were calling the draftees "zombies". They thought those men ought to be sent to jail because they were not reporting at once after what had been said to them by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and some of the cabinet ministers. An atmosphere had been created, and that atmosphere was inflated by prejudice. Those men who are now the champions of liberty and of fundamental rights were precisely those who were most unjust toward an honest and respectable class of our population. And they were less excusable for being so prejudiced and bigoted, because there were some exemptions for people who said they were conscientious objectors. But when a farmer was honest enough to say that he was not a conscientious objector, he was called a zombie, and had "traitor" written on his brow by those men
