I do not bother anyone and I do not want to be bothered by anybody; I want to have my peace. If these fellows annoy and disturb people they are acting against the provisions of some by-law or regulation and they are arrested.
Then take the padlock law of the province of Quebec. I can tell you what happened there. Mr. Lapointe was Minister of Justice and he was of the opinion that the law should be repealed. I did not think so and I sent a memorandum to the Prime Minister and told him that he would have to choose between
Cardinal Villeneuve and Tim Buck. That is why that legislation was not disallowed. Cardinal Villeneuve was a greater man than Tim Buck. Cardinal Villeneuve's successor was a chaplain in the army and he did not sign the famous list that I read not long ago. That is history.
Do you not think that reform should start at home? Do you not think that the great trouble about freedom is that very few people think? Most people are ready to accept canned ideas, and the proof of this is in the list I read. A committee on human rights will not change anything that interferes with the freedom of man. What men and women have to do is to be introspective. They must banish the fears they have, the fear of losing patronage, the fear of losing personal advantage, the fear of losing something. Most people abdicate their right to think in order to gain some personal advantage. Everybody knows that is right.
We hear reference to the freedom of the press. I remember when King Edward VIII was being married the English press said that it was self-censored. The people of Canada are self-censored about everything. They are afraid to do anything; they are too shy. Is that liberty? Is that freedom? We need to think. Privately they tell us, "You are right;" openly they tell us, "You are wrong." What could be done by the committee to correct that? What the Canadian people need is a closed retreat where they can examine their souls and realize that reform must -take place within each individual. When the individual reforms himself he will be much happier.
I have not treated this matter in a political way. I believe that all members should unite together to prove that they are not so credulous and so gullible as to swallow silly legislation like this which has been inspired by communists to destroy order in this country. When I see men of the intelligence of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), men of the intelligence of the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell); men of the intelligence of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), men of the intelligence and genius of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King); men of the intelligence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) getting together to do what Fred Rose proved in this house time and time again, I am discouraged.
Will there be a time when those who have great responsibilities in this country realize that the time has come when they have no right to be so credulous or to impose such a waste of time on the members of parliament by the creation of a committee on so-called
Human Rights

human rights which will eventually destroy the rights of all by giving undue privileges to disorderly elements in this country?

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make just a few brief observations directed to just one point in this discussion. I shall not be nearly as exciting and certainly not nearly as long as the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot).
I sympathize to some extent with those who say that the mere writing down in legislation of our rights, not only does not extend them but may even confine them. I sympathize with those who go back to the words of the poet and say that they want that freedom which-
. . . slowly broadens down From precedent to precedent;
-and is not contained in statutes.
Nevertheless I think that in these days when we are subjected to such a flood of statutes which are confining our liberties in many ways we can be thankful to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has drawn our attention to these things and who has suggested to us that we had better have a good look at them and not assume that methods and measures which have been sufficient in the past will necessarily be sufficient for the future.
My reason for rising this evening is merely to deal with one aspect of this matter, and that is the international aspect. In particular my purpose is to ask a question of the Minister of Justice, who is a serious man and whose words are taken at their face value as the words of few men are in this house. I want to ask him whether the international aspect of this thing is a serious matter or whether we are just playing with it. If one reads what he said the other evening, and I think he must have been very uneasy in some of the things he said, it seems to me that perhaps unwillingly, perhaps unintentionally, by the reading of the letter from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) explaining why we had done nothing he slipped into two things that I doubt very much he wished to slip into. This letter says that the reason for the delay, the reason which makes it impossible, I understand, for anything to happen at the next meeting of the international body is that we have gone past the date, and this letter of April 1, 1948, is a letter of delay. There are two reasons given for that delay: first of all, the government wished to refer this matter to parliament, and, further, that there had been no opportunity to discuss it as yet in parliament.

I submit that both of those reasons are trivial reasons. They are really not the kind of reason we ordinarily get from the Minister of Justice for any of the things that he puts forward, for the government have not made us ordinary members feel that they really consider it necessary to come to us very often when they want to do anything. They have rather made us feel that they can go ahead very much on their own and tell us as, if and when they feel like it. Further, I think that anyone would say that if there had been any genuine desire on the part of the government to have this matter come up in parliament some weeks ago it could easily have come up. Surely for that reason, if for no other, we might have deferred the excise taxes bill. That would simply have been a matter of extending its illegality for a few weeks longer, and if the illegality of those taxes did not trouble the government at their inception I do not see why they need have been bothered at the continuance of that illegality for a few weeks longer.
I think we are entitled to know from the Minister of Justice, who is a serious man, whether this thing means anything. I have in my hands the Canadian Bar Review and I have looked at what is proposed to be done. I have looked at the draft international declaration and at the draft international covenant, and no one is likely to say that these are things which can be taken up in a lighthearted manner. They are very difficult things. It is outside our usual field perhaps to do these things, and the only reason I suppose we would contemplate doing them at all is when we reflect on what has happened in this world we live in during the last thirty years. I was thinking today of an incident that happened, which those who have had the misfortune to be as old as I will recall, in 1913 at Zabern. It is almost impossible to believe that a single act of brutality committed by a Prussian officer in Alsace could have rocked the whole world. I will read in a sentence what happened:
In November, 1913, Zabern was the scene of a fracas which caused great bitterness in France and assumed the proportions of an international incident. A German lieutenant named Forstner grossly insulted Alsatian recruits, and a street riot followed. Twenty-nine persons were arrested. On December 2, Forstner caused the arrest of a boy at Zettweiler and struck him with his sabre. The affair led to a vote of censure on Bethmann-Hollweg in the Reichstag, but the military party secured the acquittal of Forstner on appeal to the war council.
Bethmann-Hollweg was the German Chancellor, I believe, at the time, and the vote of censure took place in the Reichstag, in what was then a real parliament. The only reason

Human Rights
I have read that is that we should remind ourselves that thirty-five years ago in this world it was possible for a single act of brutality committed in Alsace, then under German occupation, so to exercise public opinion throughout the whole world that it produced a crisis in the German government, and it is hardly too much to say that it shook the world. It seems almost incredible, almost like a fairy tale, because today you could have thousands of people killed and it would not shake anything.
It is interesting also to recall in Churchill's book on the life of his great ancestor, the Duke of Marlborough, that in the eighteenth century even war was partly civilized. The book says that in the eighteenth century the nations in peacetime did each other as much good as possible, and in wartime they did each other as little harm as possible.
It seems like a fairy tale. The only reason I mention it is that we should remind ourselves that we have moved back into the dark ages. That is where we are. and if there is anything that can possibly be done in the international sphere to serve mankind we should not regard it as a joke. It is not a joke. This is the most desperately urgent thing that could ever engage our attention, and so I ask the Minister of Justice, who is a serious man, whether he takes this matter seriously. We should not have it brought to us at all if it is not taken seriously, and if it is taken seriously we ought seriously to consider it.
The task is almost superhuman; I admit that. It may be that we should just say we cannot do it and that we should consider it no more; but before we say that I suggest that we should remind ourselves that if we do not do it, if we do not at least try to do it, sooner or later I think the third world war will come unless we can prevent it by some kind of vital association which we must take seriously. You will remember what happened to the league of nations. Why did it fail? Because people were bored with peace. They did not like peace. Peace is a dull thing. People get excited only in wartime. You could not get anyone to work for the league of nations society except longhaired cranks like myself, people who were regarded as queer people. We were told that people are combative, that they always have been, and that a second world war was sure to come. A lot of people were saying that who had never done anything themselves in the first world war. Now we have had a second world war, and many think we are to have a third world war. I do not know whether this thing is any good at all, but I think we are at least entitled to hear from the Minister of Justice whether he thinks it is a good thing.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this evening the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) attempted to put on record a long list of names, and the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) succeeded in putting them on the record. I think in fairness, not so much to the three members of the house whose names were included and who can look after themselves, but to those who are not members of the house, the country ought to know exactly what these people subscribed to, and for that reason I am going to complete the record by quoting from their statement in support of a bill of rights:
The protection of the liberties of the subject has from time immemorial been the historic responsibility of parliament.
The constitution of Canada, of which the B.N.A. Act is the principal written part, is a constitution "similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom," and embraces by implication but nowhere expressly sets forth in binding and written form such fundamental freedoms as freedom of speech, religion, assembly, press and association, nor does it afford protection for the individual against arbitrary arrest, seizure and excessive bail, and other like civil liberties and human rights.
Recent events in Canada and throughout the world have demonstrated that it is desirable that such rights be stated with the utmost clarity in the written constitution of Canada, namely, in the B.N.A. Act, in order that all men and women in Canada shall know them and shall feel that their rights are secure from interference by legislative or administrative action, through the protection of the courts.
We therefore urge that the parliament of Canada should by resolution seek an amendment to the B.N.A. Act, restraining the parliament of Canada and provincial legislatures from making or enforcing any laws abrogating the aforementioned liberties and, in particular, any laws interfering with freedom of religion, freedom of speech and expression, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, freedom of association and organization, protection against excessive bail, protection of minorities, protection against cruel and unusual punishment and protection against arbitrary and abusive deprivation of life, liberty or property, and providing against the exile of Canadian citizens, establishing the above rights and the right to the franchise, to habeas corpus, to a fair trial with the assistance of counsel, all without discrimination as to race, sex, language or religion.
Parliament has recently approved the charter of the united nations which declares it to be amongst the purposes of the united nations to promote and encourage respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion.
It would be particularly timely when recent events have left in the minds of our people a vivid sense of the dangers of totalitarianism and the repression of civil liberties, and when the parliament of Canada has recently defined Canadian citizenship, that a solemn and explicit declaration of these fundamental freedoms hitherto implicit in our traditions, should now' be enacted as part of our constitution. These rights would be in addition to, and in no way
Human Rights

in derogation from existing minority rights already set forth in the B.N.A. Act.
We urge that the members of parliament of all parties should seize this opportunity to establish a bill of rights for all Canadians.
That is the statement which was subscribed to by the men and women whose names were placed on record earlier this evening. I for one, in common with these people, believe that there is need for a charter, for a bill of rights. That is not only self-evident, I think it is overwhelming. We are living today in a time of great stress. In some parts of the world it is almost hysteria. Here at home, and abroad, men are being driven to unreasonable and excessive acts, almost to the point where they besmirch the very cause they believe in. No matter where you look, from every corner of the world, Bogota, India, Palestine, yes, in Canada, we receive reports of almost meaningless violence. We Canadians have become accustomed, yes, I think we have become indifferent to acts of violence in distant lands, and last week we had occasion suddenly to find ourselves startled from our complacency and deeply disturbed by danger signals at home. We should be all disturbed by the undemocratic behaviour of the students in the city of Windsor. No Canadian can condone such an attack on civil liberties. A mob is a mob, whether it is in Canada or in Bogota; and for us to close our eyes to certain goings on seems to me an incentive to others who are tougher than these students to see if they cannot try it, since it seems to be easy to get away with; and one excess leads to another. It is obvious in the world today that there is a division between the attackers and the defenders, and the battlelines on ideological grounds are already being drawn.
We in Canada have always been well aware of the dangers of the extreme right and the dangers of the extreme left. We know that the extreme right led us to one war. Now the extreme left has at least the possibilities of another world conflict; and to us both extremes are hateful. We want to pursue the middle course. We have always wanted the course of freedom; but the middle course, the course of freedom has some obvious deficiencies, not the least of which is the lack of a formal instrument of freedom, a bill of rights. I am familiar with the two schools of thought who have been enjoying an academic field day on the subject for the past few years. One side wants a bill of rights written into the constitution. The other side says that in the last analysis civil rights are the result of an informed and intelligent public opinion and ' that they cannot be guaranteed by putting

them into a statute. Both sides, if left to themselves, will probably be arguing happily for the next twenty years.
The point I wish to make is that a bill of rights is not an academic subject for debating societies, but a very real and a very live one and very much needed by Canadians today. There is no fundamental law in Canada guaranteeing civil liberties; there is no fundamental law in Canada prohibiting the exercise of state power in the denial of civil liberties. Ours is a negative freedom. Free speech, for instance, is in the position where it is not forbidden; but a negative freedom is not enough. There are amongst us many minorities, racial, religious, economic and political minorities, who are profoundly upset at the present state of freedom in Canada. They see a growing spirit of intolerance manifesting itself in not just isolated cases here and there, but in mass action against whole groups; and they know full well that if discrimination can be practised against one group with impunity, it can be directed against any group.
We are not going to legislate tolerance in this country. I well remember the days when we tried to enforce temperance by daw and it was a dismal failure. In the same way prejudice may masquerade as protecting the Canadian way of life, or a crusade against reactionism or communism or any other ism with which the majority happens to disagree and is out of sympathy with. Yet defining the limits of civil liberties by law would not be an empty gesture, as one hon. member intimated. There is a great need today for a formal re-statement of the fundamental principles of individual freedom. The people of Canada want to know what their rights are. They have the right to know what their rights are. The objection raised is that this house is not competent to deal with a dominion bill of rights. We are told that it would not be constitutional. Without getting into a discussion of the constitutional law, let me say that I do not think the question is as simple as all that. It is true that, under section 92, subsection 13 of the British North America Act relates to property and civil rights in the province. But is this provision meant to cover what we understand by civil liberties? I would recall that a few years ago, in the reference re Alberta legislation- the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) referred to it; 1938 S.C.R., page XOO-the Supreme Court of Canada indicated that federal legislation was authoritative in relation to public debate and discussion.
I quite agree that it is difficult to say offhand just what the position is. But the con-

Human Rights
stitutional difficulties are no reason for sloughing off this whole thing. It is a simple matter to determine what the constitutional position is. If the Department of Justice is unable or unwilling to give us an authoritative opinion that is strong enough for us to proceed on, then the committee if given the power-and they should be given that power-can direct a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. It is quite obvious that constitutionality is a condition precedent to a bill of rights. That being the case, we ought to determine the position with the least possible delay.
It seems to me that in any issue of general public policy, the government is remiss in its duty if it fails to give leadership. This is true in regard to the matter of a bill of rights and also in regard to a subject which is closely allied to it, and which has been under discussion here today, namely, the matter of communism in Canada. It is fair to say that we continue to sit on the fence in this vital issue long after Britain, Australia and South Africa have declared themselves unequivocally. The question in the minds of a great many people in Canada today is this: Is communism to be legal or illegal? Is our bill of rights to have in it a clause denying the freedom to be a communist? These are questions which we shall have to decide before very much longer.
I have had considerable experience in dealing with domestic communism. I have more of them in my riding than there are in any other riding in the Dominion of Canada. I have met them, dealt with them and defeated them, first municipally, then provincially and finally federally. over a period of nearly twenty years. My formula has always been a simple one. I like my communists out in the open so that I know who they are, where they are and what they stand for. I have done them in on every occasion that I have come to grips with them. I give that information to the house for what it is worth.
Already in this country groups of people here and there seem to be acting as though the decision to outlaw them has already been made. The very fact that they are acting in that way does not take away from us the responsibility; it only increases the responsibility. Until we are prepared to guarantee the freedom of the individual in a broadly conceived bill of rights, supported by all the ethical and social sanctions that our society as a whole can command, we shall go ill-armed into the great ideological conflict that is only beginning to make itself felt at the present time. The danger in Canada is still small, in my opinion; still just a few isolated happenings which the majority of us deplore. But it is
something which can become embedded in our national consciousness. The way to prevent that from happening is to act now, because we cannot sit this one out. The people of Canada are looking to us for guidance, for leadership and for reassurance. It is our duty to express to them the canons of individual freedom on which our society is based.
I said I felt that the need for a charter of civil liberties is overwhelming and self-evident. The mechanics of the thing can be worked out if there is a will to do so. What we do now may avoid the need for having to do something much more drastic in the days, months, and years ahead.
I like to recall John Stuart Mill's words in his famous book on liberty, where he said that the worth of a state, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals who compose it; and that a state which dwarfs its men in order that they may be more docile instruments in its hands, even for beneficial purposes, will find that with small men no great thing can really be accomplished.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The resolution before the house, Mr. Speaker, embraces both our national and international fields. In the international field the need for a code of human rights and fundamental freedoms is indeed of immediate and urgent importance. However, it will be recognized at once that the matter of the establishment and the enforcement of such a code falls within the purview of international organizations. It follows, therefore, that Canada's utmost contribution can be made in this matter by advocating and supporting the establishment and the enforcement of such a code. Obviously the extent of Canada's influence at international councils in this and other international problems will be proportionate only to her military, economic and diplomatic strength.
I was hoping to have an opportunity to discuss the international aspect of this subject, but in view of the immensity of this field I must postpone its discussion until some other time. On this occasion I intend to limit my discussion to human rights and fundamental freedoms as these rights and freedoms affect Canadian citizens within our own country. I think it will be generally agreed by. most democratically minded Canadians that human rights and fundamental freedoms are the basis upon which our constitution, our form of government and our institutions have been built. It is my view that, even though there may be some shortcomings and imperfections in our political and organizational structure, which admittedly could stand improvement.
Human Rights

nevertheless no loyal Canadian would want to see our concept of life replaced by any other advocated in the world today.
It is with this consideration in mind that we should be discussing the principles of human rights and fundamental freedoms as far as their application in Canada is concerned. However, in line with what is being proposed in the international field by the nations of the western world it may be advisable for us to review and improve some of the laws in our own country. To use but one example, I would point out that in the economic field human rights and fundamental freedoms have never been known to all our people. In other words, the economic freedom which all our people should enjoy is measured, under the present financial system, by the amount of money they can afford to spend. No one will deny that there is plenty of room for improvement in this regard. We know, too, there are numerous other things that cry out for improvement. However, the matters I have mentioned have not been the central theme of the many advocates of human rights and fundamental freedoms; it was something else that brought on the alarm. What is more, as far as human rights and fundamental freedoms are concerned, everything seemed to be running quite smoothly until Mr. Igor Gouzenko appeared on the scene with his famous bundle of documents. Now and then there might have been casual references by jurists, scholars and legislators to instances where our laws should be improved, but there was definitely no general alarm about this matter. Even during the war years, when the Canadian government did many things that revealed poor judgment or lack of knowledge in dealing with certain important matters, the general public recognized that those were abnormal times, and in view of that fact no particular protest was raised by anyone. As a matter of fact, as time went by, some of those blunders were corrected, others were forgiven and still others are being lived down by persons who were thus affected.
It was not these things that brought about the crisis in the matter of civil liberties. It was not these things that brought into the fold of the civil liberties branches many well-meaning but misled Canadian citizens. It was the clamouring of persons who were selling out the freedoms of the Canadian people that brought about this alarm, the demand for wider freedom so that they could continue their work of treason undisturbed. Yes, it was not until Gouzenko forced those famous

documents upon this government and a number of suspected persons were rounded up and detained for questioning, that human rights and fundamental freedoms began to receive so much attention. Surely it must be plain by now to most Canadians, whom this spy ring was serving and what were the intentions of the people involved.
Ah, but the critics of the procedure of the government in dealing with this problem would say, "Prosecute them in a court of law". The critics of the government in this regard may have a point there; but I wonder what procedure they would have followed if they had been in the position of responsibility, faced with the unprecedented situation that existed at the time of the unfortunate incident, when cells of agents were discovered to be in the service of a foreign country, agents who had spread their networks into various phases of activity in this country. Would they have taken a course of delayed action by providing an opportunity for persons held for questioning to get together and agree to withhold certain information? After studying the evidence carefully, it appears to me that the matter of the prosecution of suspected persons was of secondary importance as far as that situation was concerned. I may be mistaken, but it seems to me that the most important factor entering into this whole matter was to learn what information and how much was transmitted to interested parties. This consideration would appear to me to override everything else; for, after all, there are no torture chambers in Canada; no third degree methods are used here; and the slight inconvenience which may have been suffered by a few persons who kept company with dangerous characters may serve as a warning to others not to fall into the same trap.
Perhaps those learned in the law could show that I am mistaken on this point. They might be able to propose a method by which any such crisis could be avoided in future. If they can suggest a sound procedure for dealing with such matters I shall give them my support; but I have yet to hear any sound procedure suggested. I am convinced that the Canadian public would lend their support to any suggestion which would have the effect of improving our laws; but it must also be kept in mind that any such improvement should provide proper protection for this nation against treachery, deceit and treason. At no time should our laws be fashioned in such a way as to make it convenient for foreign agents to use them as a protective cloak for espionage activities.

Human Rights
In this connection I might mention that last Friday evening, after this debate was adjourned,
I met a Progressive Conservative member outside this chamber; and before we parted he made a casual statement which I consider profoundly true. He said, "Any person who needs a bill of rights to hide behind is a poor type of citizen to have in this country". There is much wisdom in that statement. If I may go on from there, in the report of the royal commission on the espionage activities we find the following passage:
The evidence has revealed the existence of an organization constituting at least a threat to the safety and interests of the state, as evidenced by the fact that some witnesses holding strategic positions have made the significant statement under oath that they had a loyalty which took priority over the loyalty owed by them to their own country, and for that reason they acted as they did, and would unquestionably have continued so to act had they not been detected.
It is a terrible state of affairs, Mr. Speaker, when some Canadians say they owe a higher loyalty to some outside power, in preference to their own country. The shocking reality of this whole situation lies in the fact that these are not simple, agitated folk who, through ignorance or economic conditions, parrot what someone else has said or make threatening remarks to make themselves more important. These young people had better than average opportunities, as their educational standings and their preferred positions indicated.
Canada and the Canadian people have been kind to these persons and placed them in positions of trust. These are the type of persons who normally would be expected to provide leadership to their less fortunate brothers. But what do we find? It is clear from the evidence that Canada and the democratic concept of life is not their ideal. The ideal which was sold to them was the nazi-fascist dictatorship, wrapped up in a red coat. While this was going on, such men as John Robert Osborn of Winnipeg, Manitoba, gave their lives in defending Canada. I might add that John Robert Osborn was awarded the Victoria Cross posthumously for his gallantry at Hong Kong. He left five orphans and a widow. I should mention also that in addition to his service in the recent war he also served in the first great war.
I would suggest, therefore, that when we are discussing this subject of civil liberties we should think of Osborn and others who have given their lives on the battlefields so that the torch of freedom may continue to burn in Canada.
A press report on this heroic role played by John Osborn says:
Time and again he picked up flying Jap grenades being hurled at his position and threw them back at the enemy with reckless disregard for his own safety. Finally a grenade fell too far away, and he had only time to smother it. It exploded just as he covered it, and he was killed. His body stopped the flying shrapnel from seriously wounding any of his companions.
In fairness to our fighting men, and particularly in fairness to the memory of those who have died in battle, we owe it to their memory and to their widows and children to stop all those who would sell out the freedoms of this country. There is no room for soft pedalling or appeasement in dealing with treachery.
Last Friday night the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) introduced a resolution dealing with this subject of human rights and fundamental freedoms. His statement, so far as any human rights bill for Canada is concerned, was significant. It was significant because he had no definite proposition to make.
First, the minister read the resolution into the record. He then reviewed the dates on which last year's committee on human rights sat, and said that it held eight meetings and made four reports to the House of Commons and to the Senate. He then reviewed what was done in regard to the international bill of rights. He told us that all provincial governments and law deans in Canadian universities were invited to submit their views on this matter, and particularly with regard to the division of power as between provincial and federal governments. The minister told us also that some of the provinces and some of the law deans replied to the communications; others just acknowledged receipt, and some did not even bother to reply.
Finally the minister told us that he had no bill to present to the house; but since an undertaking was given last year that the committee would be set up this year, the minister wanted to keep his word. Well, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but agree with the minister; and I must say I am surprised he was able to say as much as he did on the matter; for, after all, what else could he say?
So far as a bill of rights for Canada is concerned, no one has submitted a definite proposition. No doubt a bill dealing with this matter can be brought in, but only after an exhaustive study by competent jurists and other men interested in this subject. It is a task, however, which requires considerable
Human Rights

research, and it will take considerable time to complete it. The matter must also be settled with the provinces.
So the minister could hardly do other than he did when he failed to promise anything on this matter. I feel I should add this, that the main reason the minister and the government placed the resolution before the house was to silence the demand of civil liberties associations and, when the committee on human rights is set up, to throw the matter into the lap of that committee.
In view of what I have said thus far, some hon. members may think I am speaking in defence of government policy in dealing with this matter. But nothing could be farther from the truth. It is my view that the government should be given the severe verbal thrashing which they deserve. But they should be taken to task on another count. When the spy ring was uncovered I was sure that the chief spokesmen of the opposition parties would have the government over a barrel. Here was a situation where able young Canadians occupying positions of trust betrayed their country. Here was a situation which developed as a result of the government's lackadaisical policy. Here \yas a situation where the government appeased communists at every turn, and in fact entered into an unofficial arrangement during the Grey North by-election and the general election in 1945. Here was a situation where communists were actually treated as a privileged class in Canada.
Was the government not aware that, while we were being entertained by the various friendship leagues, the Trojan horse was being ushered in? Prominent Canadians and government representatives took a leading part in these powwows. And I might say this affair did not stop there. What is more, a foreign citizen had to beg the government and to plead with them to take the documents and to do something about the situation that developed in Canada.
But the government told him to go away. Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable why the opposition critics did not take the government to task on this score. But what do we find? Instead of being alarmed about the danger, the opposition critics and other civil liberties champions lashed out at the government for inconveniencing a number of persons who were held for questioning. Evidence of conflicting loyalties, evidence of infiltration of agents in a foreign service, evidence of the workings of fifth column groups in Canada did not worry the champions of civil liberties. They were concerned about the complaints of detained persons. Let me emphasize that civil liberties
must and should be protected, but the champions of civil liberties must also admit that by doing so we must not place the liberty of the entire nation in jeopardy. Under foreign domination we would have no say about civil liberties; or about anything else for that matter. In other words, our civil liberties'and our national liberties should both be protected. But to champion civil liberties at the risk of losing our national liberty is to render a disservice to Canada and to the Canadian people. I say to the champions of civil liberties that at this stage of history the struggle is not only for the extension of civil liberties; it is also a struggle, first of all, for our own national survival.
Does it not seem strange to us that this alarm for civil liberties can be found only in Canada, in the United States, in the United Kingdom, in France and in a few other countries in western Europe? But what about the civil liberties in Yugoslavia, in Roumania, in Bulgaria, in Poland, in Czechoslovakia, and above all, what about human rights and civil liberties in the U.S.S.R.?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I want to put myself clearly on the side of those who believe that we should have a bill of rights for Canadians. I noted the last question of the previous speaker when he asked why it was that in countries like Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom there is the greatest amount of concern about civil rights. I feel that that is highly significant. What it means is that in those countries where we enjoy a certain amount of freedom we know its value and we want it extended and guaranteed and made secure for all our people.
The only reason I chose to intervene in this debate-after all, the case that I might make was made so much better this afternoon by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell)-was because of what happened this afternoon when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) raised a point of order with respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker). I felt that the points raised by the Minister of Justice were technically correct, but I indicated at that time that I was in wholehearted support of the substance of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I suggested to him or to some of his colleagues that it would be desirable to have another amendment moved in a form that might be in order so that we could pursue this project of having the whole question referred to the Supreme Court of Canada.

Human Rights
I consider that the government should have taken more responsibility in this matter. It seems to me that the government should have drafted a bill of rights, brought it before parliament and let us deal with it in the house and in committee. As part of the consideration of such a bill of rights introduced by the government, arrangements could have been made for it to be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, either before or after its final enactment. However, the government has not taken that course, but has chosen rather to throw the matter into the lap of parliament and in turn has asked parliament to put it into the hands of a committee.
That being the case, we do not have the right under the rules of this house to instruct the government to do anything by way of making a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada, but I am convinced that we do have the right to make sure that the special committee which is being established has the right to make recommendations, if they so choose, calling for a reference to the supreme court. As indicated by the hon. member for Lake Centre this afternoon-I want to make it clear that in part I am taking precisely the language he used in the amendment that was ruled out of order-there is, on the one hand, the possibility of referring to the Supreme Court of Canada hypothetical questions as to the extent to which there is federal jurisdiction over matters relating to the freedoms of religion, speech, press, assembly and so on, but there is also the possibility of asking that there be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada a draft bill of rights.
I contend that the committee should have the power, without making it mandatory, to discuss these two ways of attacking the problem. The committee should have the power of making recommendations, either that such questions be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada or that a draft will be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada. Since the government did not introduce such a bill, I suggest that it is up to the committee either to decide the questions to be referred or the nature of the draft bill to be referred. Accordingly I now move, seconded by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Jaenicke), the amendment which I suggested this afternoon during the discussion on the point of order, as follows:
That the following paragraph be inserted between paragraph three and paragraph four of the proposed resolution:
"That the committee shall have power to recommend (a) that there be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada such questions as in the opinion of the committee are necessary to determine to what extent the preservation of the
fundamental freedoms of religion, speech, press and assembly, aryl the maintenance of the constitutional safeguards of the individual, are matters of federal jurisdiction; or (b) that there be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada a draft bill of rights, containing such provisions as in the opinion of the committee should be included therein, to determine whether or not it is within the powers of the federal parliament to enact such a bill of rights for the Canadian people."
I am satisfied that that amendment is in order. It does not do one thing which the amendment proposed this afternoon did, namely, put the responsibility back on the government. The simple fact is that under the rules we cannot do that. But this does give the committee the green light to make recommendations along the lines suggested in the amendment.
I shall not take the time of the house to say anything more, either on the amendment or on the general subject now before us except to say that I feel we should do everything we can in this country to maintain and extend all the freedoms we now enjoy, political, civil and religious. Freedom of thought and speech, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, yes; but let us remember that far too many human beings live lives blighted and dwarfed by economic oppression. Man will not really be free until economic tyranny is no more. In my view that is the job of political democracy today, to achieve economic freedom for all.

Speaking of internationalism and the real purpose and motive of internationalism, I have made a few notes on the social credit analysis of the hidden motives behind this drive for internationalism. It is an essential strategy for world dictatorship. The central strategy is to gain the monopoly of credit and of world propaganda so as systematically and continuously to spread false doctrines and to exploit the inevitable confusion resulting from putting such false doctrines into practice. This exploitation takes the form of centralizing every kind of control, the creation of greater and greater monopolies leading to the police state, and to the final step of world government by world cartels controlled by international financiers. Some of the meshes of this international net are UNRRA, Bretton Woods, emergency food board and UNESCO, by which nations surrender control of their credit, food supplies and propaganda; in other words, a world cartel of credits, propaganda and food to be used as sanctions against any recalcitrant countries.
National sovereignty is an obstacle in the way of these international socialists and would-be dictators. An inner ring of internationalists, extending to many countries, repudiate loyalty to the country of their adoption; they give their loyalty to their international ring and its ideals. Through their control of financial policy they are able to exert a controlling influence over the governments of the country in which they live. Their plan is to replace national with corporate government, the control being within the international ring. This is the empire of international cartels, with the international financier as the emperor. With them war is a means to an end. War is "the pursuit of policy by other means." These internationalists work to a plan. Let me name some of them. Mond sets up a chemical cartel linked with Germany and America. Samuel

recommends state ownership of coal. Isaacs (Lord Reading) negotiates a war debt settlement with Wall Street, binding the British to undisclosed terms. Sieff sets up political and economic planning, using the war as an excuse to overcome opposition. Cassel finances the London school of economics to train the bureaucracy for the future world socialist state. Laski preaches class-that is civil-war. The state assumes the ownership of coal and other real assets, and international finance involves the state in dollar debt. The socialists bankrupt the state, and the international financiers foreclose on the physical assets. In the meantime the people, forced into the factories under the slogan "Work or want", are controlled by quotas and ration books, ticketed and dossiered by social security.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a brief but, I believe, absolutely true picture of the real motives behind this drive for international government, and the surrender of national sovereignty to international control.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose for which the committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms has been set up is extremely laudable. It is to consider the manner in which the obligation assumed by Canada as a signatory to the united nations charter may be implemented. It will also have the job. if I understand the terms of reference correctly, of studying and recommending ways and means of preserving in Canada these human rights and fundamental freedoms.
It is extremely important in this changing world that Canada set her own house in order. The challenge of totalitarianism makes this imperative if our democracy is to continue to flourish. I consider it important to recognize that communism is not a disease in the strictest sense of the word. It is held up by its proponents as a way of life infinitely superior to the democracy to which we have subscribed our allegiance. As Canadians we must meet that challenge in the most effective way possible. We must prove to the world that democracy is a better way of life than that which is the basis of the Russian system.
I cannot conceive of laws and regulations preventing the growth of an idea such as communism; and I must agree with the many people who hold that you cannot destroy ideas with guns. It has been tried before with but one result, the martyrdom of a cause. But I do believe that the setting up of a new social and economic order based upon the dignity of the individual can accomplish the ends desired by all democratically minded people. Canadian boys in the last war died to establish a new

Human Rights
world order based on human equality, respect for the individual by reason of his humanity, justice in every sphere of life without any barriers of colour, race or creed. Our duty as legislators is, as I see it, to bring to fruition those very principles and ideals our sons hoped to realize in the post-war world.
The united nations has made considerable progress in achieving that goal. Not the least among those achievements is the adoption of a draft of a world bill of rights issued from Geneva on December 16 last by the united nations commission on human rights which, when adopted, will become binding upon all the signatories, including Canada. The clauses in the text are as follows, and to me they appear comprehensive and to cover adequately the field of human relations:
1.	Everyone is entitled to life, liberty and equal protection under the law.
2.	Everyone has the right to freedom of information, sipeech and expression; to freedom of worship, conscience and belief; to freedom of assembly and of association, and freedom to petition his government and the united nations.
3.	No one shall be subjected to unreasonable interference with his privacy, home, correspondence or reputation. No one shall be arbitrarily deprived of his property.
4.	There shall be liberty to move freely from one place to another within the state; to emigrate and to seek asylum from persecution.
5.	No one shall be held in slavery or involuntary servitude. No one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel or inhuman punishment or indignity.
6.	No one Shall be subjected to arbitrary arrest or detention. Anyone arrested has the right to be promptly informed of the charges against him and to trial within a reasonable time or to be released.
7.	Everyone in the determination of his rights and obligations is entitled to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal and to the aid of counsel. No one shall be convicted or punished for crime except after public trial pursuant to law in effect at the time of the commission of the act charged. Everyone regardless of office or status is subject to the rule of the law.
8.	Everyone has the right to a nationality. Everyone has the right to take an effective part in his government, directly or through his representatives, and to participate in elections, free and by secret ballot.
9.	Everyone has the right to a decent living, to work and advance his well-being; to health, education and social security. There shall be equal opportunity for all to participate in the economic and cultural life of the community.
10.	Everyone everywhere in the world is entitled to the human rights and fundamental freedoms set forth in this declaration without distinction as to race, sex. language or religion. The full exercise of these rights requires recognition of the rights of others and protection by 1 aw of the freedom, general welfare and security of all.
These are fine and noble ideals and, as I see it, it is practical Christianity. But the
mere acceptance of this bill of rights is not enough. Everyone must be prepared to do everything in his power to see that the clauses are implemented not only in Canada but everywhere in the world. That is why the setting up of this committee is so important.
Democracy must be realistic, if it is to meet the problems of our day and age. If there are problems of racial and religious inequities to be solved, let the problems be met now. Putting them off until another day, and hoping that something will happen to solve these problems will never take care of the situation. Delay is dangerous particularly in this modern world of ideologies. People who are victims of discrimination of any kind are fertile soil in which the seed of communism will flourish.
I feel that this committee not only can do a great deal to solve the problem of discrimination but may serve as well as an instrument through which problems of human rights as they affect the Indian in Canada, Chinese, Japanese, negroes and certain religious denominations may be placed squarely before the Canadian people. These are all important problems and must be solved. It may not always be politically expedient to grapple with such questions, but postponement of the evil day will not lessen but will increase the danger to this country as a democracy, if we fail to settle these differences within our social and economic structure. To talk about the brotherhood of man is not good enough. Envy, malice and hatred have all entered our civil and, in some cases, our personal lives, because of senseless inequalities which make barriers between one Canadian and another. Natural inequalities there may always be; but in no way do these deny the inherent equality of man, while artificial inequalities of wealth, birth, race, religion and opportunity do deny it.
Canadians ought to simplify the philosophy of life. We must convince ourselves and the world, too, that democracy works. Let us purify our system of glaring injustices which serve totalitarianism propaganda so well. Our thinking must rise above the level which looks down on the red, black or yellow man, the Jew or the new arrival from Europe. It must rise above the level that prefers lower taxes to good schools and adequate social legislation. It must rise above party politics or religious or racial feelings of superiority to accept the dictum that all men are equal, regardless of race, colour, creed or social status.
There is in the world today an angry surge of rebellion against exploitation, the misery of poverty and war. We can meet that protest by an understanding of the situation and by putting our own house in order. Corrupt privi-
Human Rights

lege at the expense of the people should not be the democratic way. Democracy has been an outstanding success for those who have enjoyed its privileges, but it must speak the language of the under-privileged if it is to win them as supporters. That is our job as legislators.
Recently, when discussing the work of the New York state fair employment commission in reducing discriminatory practices by employers, Mr. Charles Luckman of Lever Brothers stated:
Big business has a tremendous stake in securing civil liberties for every man, woman and child in the United States. It is my firm conviction that private enterprise is doomed in a country where civil liberties are ignored or forgotten or legislated against. In the process of investigating the abuses of civil liberties we found that whenever such abuses were rampant, standards of living were lowest, property yielded smaller returns in taxes and businessmen usually ended up in bankruptcy courts. Loss of civil liberties has invariably been followed by poverty, ignorance, and ill-health-three scourges which kept people from being good customers. Democracy is good for business.
Yes, business has a big stake in securing civil liberties for every man, woman and child. But every Canadian who enjoys our democratic way of life also has a big stake.
Our way of life today is being challenged, and we can meet that challenge if we but try. The pattern of our laws must follow the Christian concept. We have nothing to fear if we follow the teachings of Christianity, for they have stood the test of time.
In closing, I should like to direct the attention of the house to a short statement made by Edwin Markham which may serve as a guide in the committee's deliberations. He said:
We have committed the golden rule to memory; let us now commit it to life. We have preached brotherhood for centuries; we now need to find a material basis for brotherhood. Government must be made the organ of fraternity, a working form of comrade love.

speechtext:
I am grateful to Your Honour for upholding the dignity and rules of the house, but I hope you are not suggesting that I need protection from these little boys over here.
What I am anxious to say is that it seems to me that we shall serve a great deal of time in this committee. We have been told that we are to leave here at the end of June. Between now and the end of June there are two or three by-elections coming up and I for one am going to be away from here for a short time. What I have in mind is this. If we are really serious about this thing-the hon.
Human Rights

member for Winnipeg North Centre will like this even though he made some nasty cracks before he finished-why do we not first settle the question of the authority which we or the committee may exercise, instead of spending over two or three months in the committee and probably ending in a blind alley. That seems to be simply common sense. I know that somebody will immediately rise and assert the dignity of the high court of parliament, but we all know that our legislation is always subject to review by the Supreme Court of Canada if a position is created where it may be taken there.
It is a well-known constitutional fact that an opinion may be sought from the supreme court by way of question. That would mean perhaps a delay until another session. I have no idea at the moment how busy that court may be, nor do I know how long it would take to prepare and properly present the argument. I have a suggestion to make. The greatest authority on rules that I know of is the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), and I think we might excuse him while he argued this case for parliament before the Supreme Court of Canada. Now that the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre has been ruled out of order on technical grounds, which I respect, sir, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has moved an amendment in language which may be more appropriate because he learns by the best of rules, that of trial and error- I do not want to credit him with being too great a genius, for I think he learned something from the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre-why can we not agree to find out if we are right or wrong?
We have had nothing written into our constitution since 1867 dealing with this question. We are now in 1948, and surely it can wait another year if it would take that long to decide it. I am quite sure that we could not get a finding from the supreme court by the end of June in time for us to do anything about it in this House of Commons this session. Why can we not all get together and adopt that simple suggestion? If the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is not in proper form, let us put it in proper form and find out just what authority we have, instead of having a lot of us sitting around a table, making big speeches and talking all this idealistic business and some members not appearing in the committee at all because engaged perhaps on other duties, or something of that kind. Let us find out what our authority is, and then, when we know what it is, let us move within our authority just as far as we can. I submit to you, sir,

with great respect that that is the common-sense view to take of the whole position that we are in now. Then we may accomplish something, instead of delaying the situation for another year by forming the committee now.
I do not doubt that every member of the house is in favour of these freedoms and these liberties. The only difference I have heard in the house today was that raised by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), but he is an agreeable sort of gentleman and I think he might come along with us. He is the only person I have yet heard express a view against having something written into the constitution, but I do not think he would maintain that position long, because to write it in could not hurt the liberty situation; it could not hurt the basic freedom situation. The worst you could say about it would be that at the end it might be nugatory and accomplish nothing, but even at that we should have lost no ground.
So, with the greatest deference and respect I submit to the government and the minister in charge of this measure that they give it just a little more consideration. The supreme court are not so busy. We do not owe them anything. We vote their salaries in this House of Commons. They are fine men, able men, and I think they would be delighted to determine this jurisdictional question once and for all. Then we might have a committee of this house which would get some place. More than that, I suggest that the sensible thing is first to find out what we may do before we attempt to decide what we shall do, not knowing whether we have a right to do it or not.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to read an essay; I hope I shall not have to indulge in a lot of dialogue, and I shall finish by eleven o'clock.
I wish to refer to the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and to the resolution to which it refers. The object of the resolution is to find out what is the legal and constitutional position in Canada with respect to human rights, and what steps, if any, it would be advisable to take or to recommend for the purpose of preserving in Canada respect for and the observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
I suggest to the government and to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) that it is not only his right but his duty to bring in a bill of rights. I think citizenship means very little if it can be qualified from province to province and subtracted from and denied on

Human Rights
certain grounds. Two years ago we had introduced to this house a Citizenship Act, of which we were all very proud, and we did not go to the provinces to ask them whether we had the right to pass such an act. We did not write to all the deans of law schools in Canada or to the attorneys general. We passed the Citizenship Act and it has never been challenged.
Last year when I was on the committee of human rights I thought it a strange procedure that we should search out all the objections to doing something if we really intended to fulfil our covenant with the united nations. In the summary which the minister gave the other day of the replies which he had received I found very little trace of objections. It was not a summing up of objections so much as a summing up of indifference, a summing up of ignoring. If this had been a burning question of vital importance to the provinces we would not have had the minister going over one reply after another and saying that such-and-such a one had expressed no opinion, and that another was simply an acknowledgment of his_ letter without stating any grounds. It was, as I say, a summing up of indifference to, rather than a summing up of objections to, a bill of rights. I think it was an irregular thing to do, because in this house if we think we are on solid ground we pass a bill and then wait for it to be challenged, instead of going out and asking for the challenge first. The customary thing is to pass an act, and then if it is declared ultra vires by the court we must abide by that decision. But in order, I think, to appease certain people we have reversed the procedure in this case.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that citizenship and the bill of rights are associated in law and in practice and in justice and that they must be considered jointly and on the same grounds. Since we passed the Citizenship Act, we have had some violations of our basic freedoms. The right of assembly has been violated, and I regret very much that the first violation of this right of assembly took place in the province from which I come. I regret very much that it took place in Regina where a group of citizens broke up a meeting that was called under the protection of the law. If the Labour Progressive party is an illegal organization we should say so. Until it has been declared illegal, we have no right to condone the breaking up of any meeting by force, because the right of assembly is just as basic as the right of religious freedom and the right of freedom of speech. The violation which occurred in Regina was repeated in the city of Windsor. I regret that, too. I am afraid 5849-184
these young people have heard their parents say at home what they think should be done with the communists. Very often older people are irresponsible and they make rash and extravagant statements, knowing that they will not act on them, but then their teen-age children go out and act on them. Maybe that is what happened in this case.
I hold no brief for the communist party, and the party with which I am associated is unalterably opposed to the methods and doctrines of the communist party. That is true of every party in this house. There is not a party in this house that would defend the communist doctrine or practices. What is it that we must oppose in this doctrine of communism? Is it not this denial of protection to the individual, this denial of human freedom and human dignity? When we condone lawless acts of violence, acts that violate the method of democracy, then we are condoning the very essence of communism. That is why I believe in Canada we must have a bill of rights. I believe that we must set out in statutory form the things which we wish to protect and the method by which we propose to do so.
There have been not only violations of freedom of assembly in Canada but other things as well. I wish that my hon. friend, the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) and the other hon. members to my left had protested the action that took place in Alberta not so long ago where a woman in the middle of her washing, the president of the I.O.D.E, had her home invaded by the mounted police who searched for papers.

subtopic: FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS-OBLIGATIONS UNDER UNITED NATIONS CHARTER-APPOINTMENT OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I do not think there was any reason to search the premises of the president of the I.O.D.E. If the I.O.D.E. is an illegal society I have not heard of it. I object to these violations of the privacy of [DOT] the homes of individuals. I object to the violation of religious freedom; I object to the denial of the right of people to exercise ordinary human rights because they are coloured-because they are Chinese or because their ancestors were negroes-and yet these violations have taken place across Canada. It is time that we began to insist that this is a democratic country and that we intend to defend and enforce these human rights.
Recently in Europe we had an example of the observance of the rules of decency and law in the trials of war criminals whose acts provided an example of the most horrible and
Human Rights

degrading human bestiality yet on record. These people were tried and sentenced under a method that demonstrated, as nothing else could have done, the difference between the rule of law and the rule of brutality. Is that not the basic difference between the system which we defend and the system which we resist? Is not this building up of law as an entity, this building up of a method through which it might be practised, that demonstrates the value of democracy? It is time that we set up in a bill of rights a code and a method for the protection of the individual.
Referring again to our citizenship act, I have been pleased, since the passing of this act, to notice that the British government is studying it, that the government of Australia is studying it. Throughout the commonwealth it is held up as a model. That is something of which our country should be very proud. We should now pass a bill of rights which would compare with our Citizenship Act in defining the basic rights and freedoms which it would guarantee to the individual. It is time that we did this.
It is wrong to suggest that provinces may encroach upon the rights of the federal government in this respect. Recently I have had occasion to study in detail the history of the Canadian constitution. I was surprised to find that in the beginning, when the rights of the provinces were set out as opposed to the rights of the federal government, the federal rights defined by the British North America Act were used in the beginning only for illustrative purposes. They were used to illustrate the territory which should be exclusively under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. As time went on, through judicial decision, we find the provinces encroaching on the rights of the federal government. In that undefined
and unexplored legislative territory we find that the provinces made more gains than the federal government did, and gradually the only rights remaining to the federal government were those that had been originally set out for illustrative purposes only. I think it is a false conception of the federal system of government to assume that provinces can limit human freedom and human rights and can lessen the protection of the citizens of this country. Therefore I would suggest to the government that they waste no time in framing and introducing in this parliament a bill of rights. Canada is now not only a great, economic and military power but is a great moral force in the world today, and we wish to have this moral force unqualified by subtractions or limitations throughout the length and breadth of our land.
